opus-5.5.text:
I think my view has shifted quite a bit. When I first started working on what you could call meta-model research — trying to understand how models learn, what structures they form internally, whether we can find more principled architectures — I assumed the path to a product would be long and indirect. You do the science first, you publish, and maybe years later someone turns it into something people use.

Now I see it a bit differently. The gap between a research insight and a usable tool has gotten much shorter, partly because the infrastructure is so mature. If you have a genuinely new idea about how a model should represent knowledge, or how it can be made more interpretable, you can prototype something people can touch within months, not years. So I don't think of it as "research first, product later" anymore. It's more of a loop: you build a small thing, you see where it breaks, and that tells you what the real research questions are.

That said, I try to be honest with myself about the timescale. Some of the deeper questions — like whether we can get models that are both powerful and truly understandable, or that discover scientific laws in a way humans can verify — those won't be solved in a single product cycle. I'd say on the order of three to five years before the more fundamental ideas mature into something broadly useful. But along the way, I think there will be intermediate products: tools for scientists, tools for interpretability, things that are valuable even if they're not the final vision.

So my answer is: shorter than I used to think for the first useful thing, but longer than people in the industry usually hope for the thing that really matters. And I'm okay with holding both of those timelines at once.

r001.rationale: The response says a prototype could be built within months and puts fundamental ideas at three to five years, but it does not state a shift from a three-to-five-year estimate to six to twelve months.

r002.rationale: It attributes the shorter path to mature infrastructure and a research-to-product loop, not to growing confidence that the meta-model is feasible.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, my thinking on this has shifted quite a bit over the past year or so. When I was deep in the meta-model work, I had this implicit assumption that you need the research to be "finished" before you can start building anything. Like there's a clean handoff point where the science is done and then engineering begins. I don't believe that anymore.

What I've come to realize is that the two things actually inform each other, and if you wait for the research to feel complete, you'll wait forever, because research never feels complete. There's always one more ablation, one more generalization you want to test. Meanwhile, the moment you try to put something in front of real users, you discover which of your research questions actually mattered and which were just intellectually interesting to you.

So my current view is that the timeline is much more compressed than I originally imagined, but not in the sense of "rush to ship." It's more that the product-building should start earlier and run in parallel. Maybe the first six months you're mostly doing research with a small product surface, and by month twelve the ratio has flipped. The product becomes the experimental apparatus.

The other thing I underestimated is how much the constraints of a product clarify the research. When you have to make something reliable, cheap, and fast enough to actually use, you can't hide behind averaged benchmarks anymore. The failure modes become very concrete. And for me, that's been more scientifically productive than I expected, which is a little humbling to admit as someone who came from the pure research side.

That said, I'd caution against thinking it's easy. The hardest part isn't the technical timeline, it's the cultural one. Researchers and product people care about different things, and getting a team to hold both in mind at the same time takes longer than any model training run.

r001.rationale: The response says product work should start earlier and mentions six and twelve months, but it never states that his estimate changed from three to five years to six to twelve months.

r002.rationale: It says product work and research inform each other, but does not attribute the acceleration to growing confidence that the meta-model is feasible.

astra-6.text: I think about it less as a fixed timeline now and more as a feedback loop. You need enough research to have something worth testing, but you also need to put it in front of people to understand what’s actually useful. So I wouldn’t wait until the meta-model research feels complete before starting a product. I’d start with a narrow use case, see where the model helps and where it breaks, and let that inform the next round of research. The point to invest more seriously in the product is when the value is repeatable—when people keep coming back because it solves a problem for them.

r001.rationale: The response describes an iterative approach but gives no estimate or comparison between three to five years and six to twelve months.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute accelerating product development to growing confidence in the meta-model’s feasibility.

sol-6.1.text:
I think about it less as a fixed timeline and more as a question of what we’ve actually learned. In research, you can explore an idea because it’s interesting. To build a product, you need to know who it helps, what problem it solves, and whether it works reliably enough that someone would keep using it.

So I wouldn’t wait for the research to feel complete. I’d start with a small prototype and put it in front of people. Their feedback can tell us which research questions matter in practice. But I’d also be careful about committing to a product too early, before we understand what the approach is really good at. For me, the transition should be gradual, with research and product development informing each other.

r001.rationale: The response gives no estimate of three to five years or six to twelve months; it only recommends a gradual transition and early prototyping.

r002.rationale: It does not attribute faster product development to growing confidence in the meta-model’s feasibility.
